title: Hard-Boiled Eggs
subtitle: Fully set white and yolk with no grey ring, the timing is everything
excerpt: A hard-boiled egg done properly has a dry, evenly set yolk with no grey-green ring and a white that holds together cleanly. It comes down to timing and an immediate ice bath.
sourceNotes: Standard British technique. The grey ring around the yolk is a well-documented result of overcooking, hydrogen sulfide from the white reacts with iron in the yolk. Avoiding it requires precision timing and a fast cool.

recipe.batchNotes: Cook up to 8 eggs in one pan. Store unpeeled in the fridge for up to 5 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keep unpeeled in the fridge for up to 5 days. An unpeeled hard-boiled egg keeps considerably better than a peeled one.

glossaryTerms.definition: A bowl of iced water used to stop cooking instantly by rapidly reducing the food's temperature the moment it comes off the heat.
The continued cooking that happens inside food after it has been removed from the heat source, driven by stored heat in the food itself.

content.text: A properly hard-boiled egg has a clean, fully set yolk that is pale yellow all the way through, with none of the grey-green ring that signals overcooking. That ring forms when hydrogen sulfide from the white meets iron in the yolk, a reaction that only happens above a certain temperature for long enough. The fix is simple: precise timing and an immediate
ice bath
to halt
carryover cooking
the moment the eggs come out of the pan.
What you need
You will also need a large handful of ice cubes for the ice bath.
Set up the ice bath

Fill the large bowl with cold water and plenty of ice. Place it next to the hob before you start. When the timer goes, you need to move the eggs into the bath within about 10 seconds, any delay allows carryover cooking to continue inside the shell and push you toward the grey ring.
Boil the eggs
Bring a pan of water to a full rolling boil. Lower the
eggs

in with the slotted spoon. Reduce to a steady boil, not a frantic one, which bounces the eggs and risks cracking them, and cook for 10 minutes for a firm yolk with a tiny soft core, or 12 minutes for a completely set yolk with no softness at all.
Do not cook beyond 12 minutes. Each additional minute increases the risk of the grey-green ring, and by 15 minutes the eggs will have a faintly sulphurous smell as well.
Ice bath and peel

Transfer the eggs to the ice bath immediately when the timer sounds. Leave them for at least 5 minutes. The shell will contract slightly from the white, making peeling much cleaner. To peel, tap each egg firmly on the worktop, roll to crack the shell all over, then peel starting from the rounded end where the air pocket sits. A thin stream of cold water helps if any bits stick.
Storing and using

Unpeeled hard-boiled eggs keep in the fridge for up to 5 days and are one of the most practical batch-cook items going. Use them halved on a salad, sliced in a sandwich with good mayonnaise and cress, mashed for egg mayonnaise, or devilled with a pinch of paprika and mustard. Peeled eggs should be stored in a bowl of cold water in the fridge and eaten within 2 days.
Troubleshooter

Grey-green ring around the yolk: the eggs were overcooked, or not cooled fast enough after cooking. Set a strict timer and get them into the ice bath the moment it sounds. Perfectly hard-boiled eggs with no ring are achievable every time with these two steps.
Whites rubbery and tough: again, overcooking. The white proteins tighten and expel moisture when overheated. Ten to 12 minutes is the ceiling; beyond that texture suffers.

Shell sticking and tearing the white: very fresh eggs peel badly. For hard-boiled eggs, an egg that is 5 to 10 days old from the lay date peels far more cleanly than a day-old egg. If you have very fresh eggs, let them rest in the fridge for a few days before hard-boiling.
Where this dish lives

The hard-boiled egg is one of the most versatile and transportable things you can make in a kitchen. It appears in British packed lunches, in Scotch eggs wrapped in sausage meat and breadcrumbed, in the classic egg mayonnaise sandwich, and on every salad bar in the country. It was a staple of wartime cooking, a reliable source of protein that requires no refrigeration for a day or two and no reheating. Making a batch of four or six on Sunday is one of the most efficient ten-minute investments in the week's cooking.
